move: Qualifies the happiness standard by calling readiness to sacrifice one's own happiness the highest virtue, and arguing that the conscious ability to do without happiness is what best secures whatever happiness is attainable.
Treats the highest good as achieved through a self-verifying faith that we can attain our proper life, without saying what that good consists in or engaging happiness.

Splits the summum bonum into virtue and happiness and ranks virtue as the unconditioned supreme good, since happiness is not absolutely good in itself but always presupposes morally right behaviour as its condition.

Argues that nothing is good without qualification except a good will, since happiness and other gifts of fortune breed pride and mischief absent a good will, which is the condition even of being worthy of happiness.

Defends the Happiness principle by holding that happiness's various ingredients are each desired for themselves as parts of the end, so that even virtue when loved disinterestedly becomes part of happiness rather than a mere means.

Defines happiness as nature's harmony with one's will and denies any ground in the moral law for a necessary link between morality and proportionate happiness, while postulating that connection as required by the pursuit of the summum bonum.

States the Greatest Happiness Principle as making an existence free from pain and rich in enjoyments the ultimate end for whose sake all else is desirable, and hence the standard of morality for all sentient creation.
Argues that because happiness rests on variable empirical data it can yield only general advisory rules of self-love, never the objectively necessary practical law that morality commands.
Identifies the highest good attainable under the guidance of reason as love towards God, arguing that this love is shared, envy-proof and the most constant of the emotions.

Concedes that securing one's own happiness is at most an indirect duty, notes that no definite conception of happiness can be formed, and insists the law is to promote it from duty rather than from inclination.

Reframes the dispute as a question of ultimate ends not amenable to ordinary proof, since anything proved good must be shown to be a means to something admitted good without proof, while insisting rational considerations can still bear on it.
Applies the utilitarian standard of the greatest amount of happiness altogether, justifying the cultivation of noble character by the happiness it produces in others even if it costs the agent.
